harbor.practice: Harbor: 8,000 employees + 1,200 customer tenants; 21,000 daily users × 6 requests, 14% in the peak hour, burst 2 → about 10 RPS at peak, about 60 in flight at 6 s each.
harbor.failure: Multiplying by a peak factor twice, or putting p99 latency into Little's law.
harbor.fitNote: about 10 RPS at peak; small numbers
harbor.tryIt: In the capacity calculator, enter 0.3 million registered at 7% active (Harbor's 21,000 daily users), 6 requests, 14% peak hour, burst 2 and 6 s per request. Check you get about 10 RPS and about 60 in flight.

store.fitNote: a holiday sale multiplies the peak
store.practice: {company} plans for its holiday sale, not an average day: 20 million registered, 10% using the assistant, 4 requests each, 15% in the peak hour and a burst factor of 3 give about 1,000 RPS at the opening minute. (Illustrative.)
store.failure: Planning from a normal week's peak and meeting the sale with a third of the capacity.
store.tryIt: In the capacity calculator, enter 20 million registered, 10% active, 4 requests, 15% peak hour, burst 3 and 5 s per request. Check you get about 1,000 RPS and 5,000 in flight. Then try burst 1.5 and compare.

bank.practice: {company}'s busiest days are salary credits and month-end statements, when balance and dispute questions jump. The plan uses those days' peak hour, measured from last year's logs. (Illustrative.)
bank.failure: Using average daily traffic and missing the month-end peak.
bank.tryIt: In the calculator, enter 12 million registered, 3% active, 2 requests, 12% peak hour and burst 2, and compute the in-flight requests at 8 s each. Then double the active share for month-end.

travel.practice: When a storm cancels flights, many {company} travellers message at once. The plan uses a high burst factor for disruption days, and the queue simulation shows how waits grow as utilisation nears 100%. (Illustrative.)
travel.failure: Sizing for normal days and treating disruption spikes as rare.
travel.tryIt: Find the day with most cancelled flights in disruptions.csv. In the queue simulation, set 4 servers and 0.5 s service, then raise the arrival rate from 6 to 8 per second and watch p95 wait.

harbor.practice: Harbor's SLOs: 99.9% availability, p95 first token ≤ 1.5 s, sampled groundedness ≥ 95%, ≤ $0.01 per resolved question, each with a written measurement boundary.
harbor.failure: Treating a sampled judge score as a complete measurement of all production answers.
harbor.tryIt: In the error-budget calculator, pick 99.9% and 2 million requests a month, then 99.99%, and note how many failures each allows. Then write Harbor's four SLIs with what each measures and what it leaves out.

store.fitNote: quality and cost SLOs beside availability
store.practice: {company} sets an availability SLO for {assistant} and a quality SLO from a daily judged sample of answers about orders and returns, so a silent retrieval bug shows up the same day.
store.failure: Having only availability SLOs, so wrong return-policy answers go unnoticed for days.
store.tryIt: In the calculator, set 99.9% and 140 million requests a month and note the budget. Then write one SLO each for availability, latency, quality and cost for {assistant}.

bank.practice: {company}'s SLA to business customers is looser than its internal SLO, and the error budget is reviewed weekly. Quality is measured on a judged sample of answers, with a written note that the sample is not every answer.
bank.failure: Promising customers the same number as the internal SLO, leaving no room before a contract breach.
bank.tryIt: In the calculator, compare 99.9% and 99.95% at 30 million requests a month. Then write an internal SLO and a looser SLA for {assistant}, and say why they differ.

travel.practice: {company} has a freshness SLO for disruption information: a cancellation must be visible to {assistant} within 5 minutes, because an answer from older data sends travellers to the airport.
travel.failure: Measuring freshness as an average, so a few hour-old updates hide behind fast ones.
travel.tryIt: Write a freshness SLI and SLO (p99 lag) for disruption updates, and an availability SLO. In the calculator, see how fast a one-hour outage uses a 99.9% monthly budget.

harbor.practice: Harbor's OCR backfill runs in its own pool and cannot take interactive inference slots; the assistant answers from the last consistent index while lag is visible.
harbor.failure: Splitting services but leaving them on one shared unbounded queue or saturated database.
harbor.fitNote: OCR backfill in its own pool
harbor.tryIt: Write Harbor's four workloads (ingestion, retrieval, generation, agents) with their latency need and scaling unit, and say which ones may share a pool.

store.practice: Before a sale, sellers update millions of listings while shoppers search. {company} runs bulk embedding on a separate batch pool, so query embeddings keep low latency and the backfill simply takes longer.
store.failure: One embedding pool for both, so a listing backfill raises search latency at the start of the sale.
store.tryIt: Estimate how long re-embedding products.csv scaled to 2 million listings takes at a batch rate you choose, and write which pool serves query embeddings meanwhile.

bank.fitNote: agent investigations kept off chat capacity
bank.practice: {company}'s dispute investigation agents draw from their own model quota, so long runs never take slots from customer chat at month-end.
bank.failure: Separate services that still share one database connection pool, which the batch job exhausts.
bank.tryIt: List {company}'s workloads with their latency needs and say which ones need their own quota or pool.

travel.practice: During a disruption, {company}'s rebooking agents run long and call suppliers often. They have their own worker pool and model quota, so chat stays responsive.
travel.failure: Letting rebooking agents hold every model slot during a storm.
travel.tryIt: Write {company}'s workload table (ingestion of supplier content, retrieval, chat, rebooking agents) with latency need and scaling unit.

harbor.practice: Harbor's hour-long imports return a job receipt; the query API reads only published index versions, never half-written chunks.
harbor.failure: A semantic cache keyed without permissions or source version.
harbor.fitNote: job receipts and published index versions
harbor.tryIt: Step through the cache-layer figure and write Harbor's exact-cache key. Then list two Harbor questions that may use a semantic cache and two that must not.

store.practice: {company} uses a semantic cache only for public FAQ answers (return windows, delivery times), with tenant and scope in the key. Anything about a specific order skips the cache.
store.failure: A semantic cache that answers “cancel my friend's order” with the answer for “cancel my order”.
store.tryIt: Take 20 chats from chats.json and mark which could use a semantic cache. For two similar-looking chats that need different answers, explain why.

bank.practice: {company} caches retrieval results for policy questions, but never caches responses that include account or case data, and every cache key includes the customer's permission scope.
bank.failure: Caching a balance answer by question text, so the next customer sees it.
bank.tryIt: Write the cache key for a policy answer and say which question types may never be cached at all.

travel.fitNote: long tasks return a task ID
travel.practice: A {company} rebooking search can take over 30 seconds across suppliers, so the API returns a task ID, shows progress and notifies the traveller when options are ready.
travel.failure: Holding the HTTP request open during supplier searches, so mobile clients time out.
travel.tryIt: Write the asynchronous flow for a rebooking request (task ID, status endpoint, notification), and decide which fare_rules.json answers could be cached and with what TTL.

harbor.practice: Harbor's gateway gives each tenant token-per-minute and concurrency quotas, weighted by estimated context size.
harbor.failure: Automatic fallback to a model that does not support the same tools or schema behaviour.
harbor.tryIt: In the noisy-neighbour figure, set tenant A's burst to 10× with a shared FIFO queue, then switch to per-tenant quotas and fair queuing, and compare the other tenants' waits.

store.practice: Large sellers call {company}'s listing-writer API from their own scripts. The gateway gives each seller a token and spend quota, so one seller's bulk job cannot slow every other seller.
store.failure: One seller's script looping on the API and raising latency for everyone.
store.tryIt: In the figure, set tenant A's burst to 20× with FIFO, then with fair queuing. Then write the quota (requests and tokens per minute) you would give a large and a small seller.

bank.practice: {company}'s gateway routes by data class: customer data goes only to in-house models, public policy questions may use a hosted model, and every route is logged.
bank.failure: Falling back to a hosted model that customer data must not reach.
bank.tryIt: Write gateway routing rules for {company}: which request types go to which backend, and which fallbacks are forbidden.

travel.practice: {company}'s corporate clients have their own quotas and a higher tier in fair queuing, so a consumer spike during a disruption does not slow travel desks.
travel.failure: Falling back to a model that does not support the same tool schema, so rebooking calls fail.
travel.tryIt: In the figure, run tenant A's burst at 10× with each scheduling mode. Then write which tenants {company} has and their weights.

harbor.practice: When the model pool saturates, Harbor serves authorised policy excerpts with a status line and pauses optional agent investigations.
harbor.failure: Unbounded queues, which trade visible rejections for long delays and cascading failure.
harbor.fitNote: policy excerpts when the model pool saturates
harbor.tryIt: In the circuit-breaker figure, toggle the provider outage and watch the breaker open and traffic go to the fallback. Then write Harbor's degradation ladder from L0 to L4.

store.fitNote: shed free features, keep checkout help
store.practice: When {company}'s sale traffic exceeds capacity, it sheds suggestions and listing rewrites first, keeps order and payment help, and rejects early any request that would miss its deadline.
store.failure: Queuing every request during the sale, so many shoppers wait past their deadline and get nothing.
store.tryIt: In the load-shedding figure, set load to 2× capacity and a 10 s deadline, and compare no shedding, shedding by predicted wait, and priority. Then write {company}'s ladder.

bank.practice: If {company}'s model pool is unhealthy, the assistant falls back to policy search results and a clear status message; it never guesses balances or case outcomes with a weaker model.
bank.failure: Degrading to a smaller model for case summaries without evaluating it on case work.
bank.tryIt: Write {company}'s degradation ladder and mark which levels are allowed for customer answers and which only for staff.

travel.practice: During a disruption, {company} drops to a mid-size model with fewer retrieved rules, pauses marketing content, and shows a status banner. The circuit breaker sends traffic to the fallback provider without waiting for timeouts.
travel.failure: Retrying a failing provider for every request, which piles up threads and slows every traveller.
travel.tryIt: In the load-shedding figure, set load to 2.5× and a 5 s deadline and compare the three policies. Toggle the outage in the breaker figure and count failed requests.

harbor.practice: Harbor fails read-only search over to a second region, but queued write actions have one designated execution owner to avoid duplicates.
harbor.failure: Assuming active-active APIs give consistent business actions across regions.
harbor.tryIt: Write RPO and RTO for Harbor's conversation store, index and ticket queue, and say which can be rebuilt and how long that takes.

store.practice: {company} runs a quarterly game day: block the primary model provider for 10% of traffic and check the fallback keeps schema and tool behaviour.
store.failure: A fallback that has never served real traffic, discovered on sale day.
store.tryIt: Plan a game-day test for {company}: what is blocked, the traffic share, what you measure, and what would stop the test.

bank.practice: {company}'s customer data stays in national regions, so failover goes only to an in-country standby. Each store has a written RPO and RTO, and restores are tested every quarter.
bank.failure: Treating a database replica as a backup, so an accidental delete is copied to it within seconds.
bank.tryIt: Write RPO and RTO for {company}'s case store, vector index and audit log, and the restore test you would run for each.

travel.practice: {company} serves from two regions active-active for read-only search; bookings have one execution owner so a failover does not create duplicate bookings.
travel.failure: Replaying queued booking changes in both regions after failback.
travel.tryIt: Write the failover and failback steps for {company}'s booking queue, including how queued writes are replayed exactly once.

harbor.practice: Harbor's load test replays logged prompt lengths with an open-loop arrival rate and a mocked model, then benchmarks the real inference pool separately; the two reports are labelled differently.
harbor.failure: Testing with empty prompts and one-token answers.
harbor.fitNote: low traffic makes load tests short
harbor.tryIt: Run the k6 laptop lab with an arrival rate of 10 per second and Harbor-like prompt lengths, and read the p95 and p99 lines.

store.practice: {company}'s sale load test replays logged chat lengths and tenant mix at an open-loop arrival rate against a mocked model, then benchmarks the real model pool separately. Each report says which it is.
store.failure: A closed-loop test that slows down with the service and reports good latency.
store.tryIt: Measure prompt lengths of chats.json messages (or use the figure's log-normal), then run the k6 lab with a ramping arrival rate. Compare p95 with fixed-length prompts.

bank.fitNote: soak tests for steady staff traffic
bank.practice: {company} runs an 8-hour soak test before each release to catch memory growth and cache bloat, plus a failure test that injects core-system latency.
bank.failure: Testing only for an hour and missing a slow memory leak.
bank.tryIt: Write a soak test and a failure test for {company}: duration, load, injected fault, and the pass thresholds.

travel.practice: {company} runs spike tests that jump from 20% to 150% of capacity in a minute, like a storm, and checks that autoscaling, queues and shedding hold.
travel.failure: Ramping slowly in tests when real disruptions arrive in a minute.
travel.tryIt: Change the k6 lab to a spike scenario (20% to 150% in one minute) against the mock, and record when requests start failing.

harbor.practice: If Harbor spends $10 on 100 tasks and 50 succeed, the figure reported is $0.20 per successful task, plus the support cost of fixing the 50 failures.
harbor.failure: Optimising price per call while completion rate falls.
harbor.tryIt: In the cost-per-success calculator, keep the defaults and compare A and B. Then set the human cost to $0 and see which option is cheaper.

store.practice: {company} found a cheaper model resolved fewer return chats, and each unresolved chat went to a paid human agent. Counting those escalations, the more expensive model was cheaper per resolved chat. (Illustrative.)
store.failure: Celebrating a lower cost per call while the resolution rate fell.
store.tryIt: In the calculator, set A to $0.003 at 60% and B to $0.009 at 88% with a $3 human cost, and compare cost per success. Then find the human cost at which A becomes cheaper.

bank.practice: {company} enforces a daily spend limit per business customer in the gateway and alerts at 50, 80 and 100%. At the limit, customers on a basic plan are moved to a smaller model.
bank.failure: One integration summarising every page view and nobody noticing until the monthly bill.
bank.tryIt: Write {company}'s budget rules per request, task, tenant and feature, and what happens at 100% for each.

travel.practice: {company}'s capacity forecast adds known events: holiday booking periods and the monsoon season, using last year's peaks and this year's growth.
travel.failure: Forecasting from the last month only and missing the seasonal peak.
travel.tryIt: Count bookings per month in bookings.csv and pick the peak month, then forecast next year's peak with a growth rate you state.

harbor.practice: Harbor's launch review states: "measured 60 RPS on staging with p95 1.8 s for this workload; projected 100 RPS with two more replicas, not yet validated".
harbor.failure: Describing a simulation or extrapolation as a system that served millions of users.
harbor.fitNote: small scale, but the labelling habit applies
harbor.tryIt: Rewrite Harbor's launch-review sentence as three labelled lines: measured, projected and actual, each with its conditions.

store.practice: {company}'s sale readiness review lists measured numbers (load test date, traffic mix), projected capacity (with assumptions) and last sale's actual peak in separate rows.
store.failure: Quoting a vendor benchmark as sale capacity.
store.tryIt: Write three rows for {company}'s sale review: a measured number with test conditions, a projection with assumptions, and an actual peak. Mark which one you would trust for planning.

bank.practice: {company} reports capacity to its risk committee with each number labelled measured, projected or actual, and with the date and conditions of every test.
bank.failure: Telling the committee the system “handles 10 million customers” when that is a projection.
bank.tryIt: Rewrite the statement “handles 10 million customers” as a measured line, a projected line and an actual line for {company}.

travel.practice: After each major disruption, {company} compares the actual peak with the projection and re-measures if the traffic mix changed.
travel.failure: Keeping an old load-test number after the prompt mix changed.
travel.tryIt: Write a launch-review table for {company} with measured, projected and actual rows, and the rule that triggers a new load test.

store.scenario: Plan for a holiday sale: state DAU, requests per shopper, peak factor and token lengths from chats.json. Load-test the mock with seller tenant skew and a provider failure, and keep measured, projected and last-sale figures in separate tables.

bank.scenario: Plan for month-end: state customer and staff traffic separately, with SLOs per workload. Load-test the mock with a core-system latency fault, and label every figure as measured, projected or actual.

travel.scenario: Plan for a disruption day using disruptions.csv: state the burst factor, rebooking task duration and supplier fan-out. Run a spike test against the mock with one supplier failing, and label projections separately from measurements.

harbor.scenario: Plan for Harbor's 21,000 daily users and 1,200 tenants: state the assumptions, compute peak RPS and in-flight requests, and load-test the mock with tenant skew and a provider failure. Label measured and projected figures separately.
